overview.main_topic: Embedding TensorBoard in a notebook, the TensorBoard metrics dashboard, and the limits of fit() that motivate custom training loops

summary:
The page first gives the Colab commands announced on p.237:

```
%load_ext tensorboard
%tensorboard --logdir /full_path_to_your_log_dir
```

In the TensorBoard interface you can monitor **live graphs of training and evaluation metrics**, as in **figure 7.7**. The screenshot shows the Time Series tab with two runs, `train` and `validation`, an `epoch_accuracy` chart over steps 0-9 (both curves rising to about 0.98), a collapsed `epoch_learning_rate` card, and a settings panel with smoothing set to 0.6.

**Section 7.4, Writing your own training and evaluation loops**, begins. The `fit()` workflow balances ease of use and flexibility and is what you will use most of the time, but it isn't meant to support everything a researcher may want - even with custom metrics, losses and callbacks. The built-in `fit()` is focused on **supervised learning**: known *targets* (also called *labels* or *annotations*) are associated with the inputs, and the loss is computed from these targets and the model's predictions. Not all machine learning fits this mould. Setups without explicit targets include:

- **generative learning** (introduced in chapter 16),
- **self-supervised learning**, where targets are obtained from the inputs,
- **reinforcement learning**, driven by occasional "rewards" - "much like training a dog".

And even in ordinary supervised learning, a researcher may want "novel bells and whistles that require low-level flexibility". The next page recaps the three steps of a training loop and announces reimplementing `fit()` from scratch.

paragraphs.what_it_says: The TensorBoard interface shows live graphs of training and evaluation metrics; figure 7.7 is an example.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Figure 7.7 shows the Time Series dashboard: runs 'train' and 'validation' (written by the callback into separate subfolders) plotted on the same epoch_accuracy chart, with a table of smoothed and raw values at the latest step (step 9 = the 10th epoch). A smoothing slider (0.6) applies an exponential moving average to the displayed curves; the faint lines are the raw values.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Seeing train and validation curves together is how you detect overfitting and choose the best epoch - the same judgement EarlyStopping automates (p.234).
paragraphs.technical_idea: TensorBoard's smoothing is an exponential moving average: $s_t = \alpha s_{t-1} + (1-\alpha) x_t$ with $\alpha$ = the smoothing value (beyond the book). In the figure, train and validation accuracy are close (~0.98 each), so there is no strong overfitting by epoch 10.

paragraphs.excerpt: After all, the built-in fit() workflow is solely focused on supervised learning:
paragraphs.what_it_says: fit() is focused on supervised learning, where known targets (labels/annotations) are associated with inputs and the loss is a function of targets and predictions. Other setups have no explicit targets: generative learning (chapter 16), self-supervised learning (targets obtained from the inputs), reinforcement learning (learning driven by occasional rewards, like training a dog). Even in supervised learning, researchers may want novel features requiring low-level flexibility.
paragraphs.what_it_means: fit()'s default train step assumes data arrives as (x, y) and computes loss(y, model(x)). When the training signal is something else - a reconstruction or adversarial objective, labels derived from the input itself, or rewards from an environment - that assumption breaks and you need to write the step yourself.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It explains why later chapters (e.g. generative models) write custom training logic, and it motivates the three-step loop reimplemented in TensorFlow, PyTorch and JAX in the coming sections (p.239 onward).
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: self-supervised learning still often has a loss of the form loss(target, prediction); the 'target' is just constructed from the input (e.g. the next token in language modelling), so the boundary with fit() is about how targets are produced rather than whether a loss exists.

concepts.name: TensorBoard
concepts.definition: Browser-based app showing live graphs of training and evaluation metrics.
concepts.significance: Figure 7.7 shows train/validation accuracy side by side.
concepts.misconception: Smoothing changes only the display, not the logged values.

concepts.name: Supervised learning
concepts.definition: Setup with known targets associated with inputs, loss computed from targets and predictions.
concepts.technical: Training step: loss = L(y, f(x)); gradients of loss w.r.t. weights; update.
concepts.significance: The only setup fit() is built around.
concepts.misconception: Not all ML has explicit labels.

concepts.name: Self-supervised learning
concepts.definition: Learning where targets are obtained from the inputs.
concepts.intuition: Making your own quiz from the textbook.
concepts.technical: E.g. predict masked or future parts of the input.
concepts.significance: Example of a setup beyond fit()'s default assumptions.
concepts.example: Predicting the next word of a sentence (beyond the book).
concepts.misconception: It is not unsupervised in the sense of having no loss target - the target comes from the data itself.

concepts.name: Reinforcement learning
concepts.intuition: Training a dog with treats (the book's analogy).
concepts.technical: An agent acts in an environment and adjusts behaviour to maximise reward; no per-input target.

concepts.name: Custom training loop
concepts.definition: Training logic written by hand instead of using fit().
concepts.technical: Forward pass -> loss -> gradients -> weight update, repeated per batch (p.239).
concepts.significance: Needed for non-supervised setups or novel research ideas.
concepts.example: Section 7.4 reimplements fit() in TensorFlow, PyTorch, and JAX.
concepts.misconception: Custom logic doesn't always mean abandoning fit(): you can override train_step (p.246).

deeper.title: What changes in each learning setup
deeper.body:
| Setup | Where the training signal comes from | Why plain fit() may not fit |
|---|---|---|
| Supervised | Given targets y for each x | It doesn't - this is fit()'s home turf |
| Generative (ch. 16) | The data distribution itself, often via several networks or special objectives | The loss may involve sampling or multiple models |
| Self-supervised | Targets built from the inputs | Targets must be constructed on the fly |
| Reinforcement | Occasional rewards from an environment | No dataset of (x, y) pairs; data depends on the model's own actions |

The first two columns follow the book; the last column is our elaboration.

deeper.title: Training a dog
deeper.body: The authors compare reinforcement learning to training a dog: you can't show the dog the 'correct answer' for every situation; you reward good behaviour occasionally and it figures out which actions led to the treat. Supervised learning, by contrast, is like correcting every single answer on a worksheet.

misconceptions.claim: Custom callbacks let fit() handle any learning algorithm.
misconceptions.correction: The authors say fit() isn't meant to support everything, even with custom metrics, losses and callbacks; callbacks act between steps, not inside the core training step.

misconceptions.claim: Self-supervised learning has no targets at all.
misconceptions.correction: It has targets, but they are obtained from the inputs rather than provided as annotations.

misconceptions.claim: The faint and bold lines in figure 7.7 are two different models.
misconceptions.correction: Beyond the book: in TensorBoard, faint lines are raw values and bold lines the smoothed version of the same run; colours distinguish the train and validation runs.
